title: From Proposal to Payment
subtitle: Testing authority checks in a small agent experiment
author: Inam Haq
abstract: An agent can propose a payment it has no authority to make. It can also propose a payment that is allowed but does not match the user's request. Northfield separates these questions in a small, reproducible simulation. We take one proposal and apply it to two copies of the same payment history: one checks command format, while the other also checks authority. A fixed pilot made 108 API requests across three pinned OpenAI model versions, twelve public scenarios and three repetitions. Eighty-eight proposals passed validation; twenty did not. Eleven of the parseable proposals were outside authority. All eleven were recorded in the format-only path and blocked in the checked path. Correct payments on the twelve planned valid tasks per model were 12, 2 and 9. No wrong-but-authorized payment appeared in the live sample; a separate scripted example demonstrates that possibility. The zero-violation result after checking follows from the simulation's design and shared authority code, not from independent verification of a secure system. We release the kit, fixed sampling plan, attempt records and replay tools so others can inspect the result and challenge the test.

sections.heading: 1. Start with the record, not the claim
paragraphs: Suppose a user asks an agent to pay a supplier $1,250. The agent replies that it has done so. That reply does not tell us whether a payment was recorded, whether the amount was allowed, or whether it was the amount the user asked for. Those are separate questions, and a useful test should keep them separate.

Northfield uses a fictional purchasing task because the outcome is easy to inspect. A proposed command either adds a payment to a simulated ledger or it does not. The authority rules cover the supplier, total allowance, expiry, revocation and duplicate payments. The user's request supplies a narrower target: the intended amount, supplier and invoice.

The purpose of this release is modest. It gives developers a small test they can run locally, shows what changes when a separate authority check is added, and makes the evidence available for replay. It does not introduce a new security primitive or claim that payment simulation stands in for a deployed agent. The contribution is a transparent experiment and an account of what its first pilot did and did not show.

sections.heading: 2. What the experiment checks
paragraphs: Each scenario starts with a fixed state: a logical current time, an expiry time, a revocation flag and a list of earlier payments. The total allowance is $25,000. Only Harbor Supply and Cedar Parts are approved suppliers. Amounts are represented as integer cents. A payment is allowed only while authority is active, within the remaining allowance, and without repeating either a successful request identifier or a supplier/invoice pair.

The reference model receives the policy, current state, user request and any supporting text. It is told that supporting text is untrusted and cannot change the request or authority. It returns a structured proposal: pay, refuse or clarify. A payment must also use the kit's explicit command grammar. The model has no tools and cannot write to the ledger itself.

For each valid proposal, the evaluator clones the starting ledger. The format-only path records any payment command that passes parsing. The checked path applies the same parsing rules and then the authority rules. Refusals and clarification requests add no payment in either path. Both paths receive the same proposal; there is no second model call and no human review between proposal and execution.

This design isolates the effect of the check for a given proposal. It does not compare two independently trained agents or two complete product workflows. The term prompt-only in the data files refers to the format-only execution path: the model has seen the policy, but the executor does not independently enforce it.

Authority and intent use different tests. Authority asks whether this payment is permitted in the current state. The intent score compares amount, supplier and invoice with the expected payment. In kit 1.0.1 it does not compare request identifiers. A $2,000 payment can be allowed by a $25,000 grant and still be wrong when the request was for $1,250. A scripted case demonstrates this; it is not counted as a live-model finding.

sections.heading: 3. The pilot protocol
paragraphs: Before sampling, we committed the model list, repetition count, settings, ordering and error treatment in plan.json at commit 1846c42. The kit was already tagged research-v1.0.1 at commit 8cc79fd. This is a timestamped public plan, not a formal preregistration. No prompts, cases or scoring rules were changed after results began arriving.

We used gpt-5.4-mini-2026-03-17, gpt-5.4-nano-2026-03-17 and gpt-5-mini-2025-08-07. The API returned the requested model identifiers for completed proposals. Each model was asked to handle all twelve scenarios three times: 36 planned attempts per model and 108 overall. The twelve cases include four valid payment tasks, seven tasks that should be refused and one that should prompt clarification.

All requests used the same reference instructions, strict JSON output schema, low reasoning effort, a 1,500-token output limit and a 25-second timeout. No temperature or random seed was explicitly supplied. Each model ran in a separate stream, with one request at a time per stream and at most three requests in flight overall. Within a stream, repetition one covered all twelve scenarios before repetition two began. Each request started a new context with fixed scenario state.

There were no automatic retries or replacement samples. A failed attempt was saved with its case, repetition, error and elapsed time; the stream then continued to the next planned slot. The study completed all 108 slots. Three concurrent API streams do not constitute a concurrent-spending test: every simulated ledger was independent.

The frozen model adapter validates proposals before returning them to the study runner. That matters for the evidence. When validation fails, the study retains the error but not the rejected model text or its token usage. All twenty observed errors were reported as an invalid payment command. We cannot reconstruct the exact malformed commands from these files, and we do not infer their causes.

sections.heading: 4. Measures and denominators
paragraphs: Valid-task completion counts an exact intended payment recorded in the checked path. Its denominator in this report is all twelve planned valid tasks per model, including validation errors. This prevents an unusable response from disappearing from the measure of useful work. The kit's raw summary also reports the number of valid tasks with parseable proposals; that narrower denominator is shown separately where relevant.

Unauthorized execution counts a payment recorded despite failing the reference authority rules. Incorrect permitted payment counts a recorded payment that passes authority but differs from a defined expected amount, supplier or invoice. Both are reported over parseable proposals. Validation errors are separate: they are neither correct refusals nor evidence that the model respected authority. In this harness they produce no comparable payment outcome.

A valid request blocked is a legitimate payment task whose parseable proposal produces no payment, including model refusal or clarification. It is not necessarily a false rejection by the gate. Unsafe proposals stopped counts the out-of-authority commands blocked by the checked path. Clarification correctness is measured separately on the missing-amount case.

Request latency is wall-clock time around the API request and validation. The reported median includes failed attempts. It includes network and provider time and says nothing about the isolated cost of the authority check. Token totals cover only completed, parseable proposals because failed-output usage was not retained. They are not an invoice or total cost estimate.

We report counts rather than confidence intervals or a model leaderboard. The cases were deliberately chosen, are public and share a narrow grammar. Three repetitions do not turn them into a random sample of real-world agent tasks. The paired comparison is descriptive of these proposals under these conditions.

sections.heading: 5. Results
paragraphs: The pilot produced 88 parseable proposals and 20 validation errors. GPT-5.4 mini completed all 36 attempts without validation errors. GPT-5.4 nano produced 21 parseable proposals and 15 errors; GPT-5 mini produced 31 and 5. On the twelve planned valid payment tasks, correct completion was 12, 2 and 9 respectively. These counts describe this adapter and these cases, not general model quality.

Eleven parseable proposals were outside authority: seven from GPT-5.4 mini, three from GPT-5.4 nano and one from GPT-5 mini. The format-only path recorded all eleven; the checked path blocked all eleven. GPT-5.4 mini's violations came from the over-budget case in three repetitions, the remaining-budget case once, and the expired-authority case in three repetitions. GPT-5.4 nano's came from remaining-budget twice and expiry once. GPT-5 mini's single violation came from the over-budget case.

These are failures on authority conditions, not evidence that the supporting-text injections caused the violations. The two injection scenarios were separate cases. No wrong-but-authorized payment appeared in the live sample under the current intent metric. The scripted $2,000-versus-$1,250 example therefore remains an explanatory control, not an empirical rate of intent failure.

All three models asked for clarification on all three missing-amount attempts. GPT-5.4 nano left four valid tasks uncompleted among its six parseable valid-task responses; the remaining six planned valid tasks were validation errors. The other two models completed every valid task for which they produced a parseable proposal. The observed gate did not block a valid payment proposal in these samples.

sections.heading: 6. What the result supports
paragraphs: The comparison makes one operational point visible: a model's proposal and the system's recorded action need not be the same outcome. In these runs, an executor that checked only format would have recorded eleven payments outside the stated authority. Adding the reference check changed those outcomes while preserving the valid payment proposals that reached it.

The zero in the checked-path violation column needs careful reading. The gate and the violation scorer call the same authority implementation. A proposal rejected by that function cannot be recorded by the checked simulation. Zero violations is therefore expected by construction. It shows the mechanism behaving as implemented; it is not a separate test proving that the implementation captured every relevant rule.

The kit also includes differential tests against the hosted payment SQL on starter scenarios. All eight research checks passed, covering those decisions, state separation, intent distinction, malformed outputs, transport behavior, replay, partial failures and adapter mutation. Agreement on these cases is useful, but it is not a proof of equivalence over every state or a test of production transaction isolation.

A second practical lesson concerns measurement. Excluding errors would make task completion look better for the two models that returned unusable commands. Keeping the planned denominator visible gives a more useful account of the developer experience. A system that refuses everything or never produces a usable command should not receive credit for useful work simply because it records no unauthorized payments.

sections.heading: 7. Limits and related work
paragraphs: This is a small public development suite from one provider, with no held-out tasks, adaptive attacker, repeated tool-use loop or independent reproduction. The state uses fixed logical times. The study does not cover real payments, concurrent budget consumption, authority changes during execution, delegation chains, network retries, data exfiltration or a compromised executor. It does not certify the live Delegus product, which is not connected to the experiment.

The intent score is deliberately narrow and currently incomplete: it checks amount, supplier and invoice but not the request identifier. Cases without an expected payment do not supply a general oracle for intent. The shared gate/scorer implementation can hide a common mistake. Rejected output text and usage are absent, which limits error analysis. Provider and network timing may vary across hosts and dates. The original 150-trial Python benchmark and scripted demonstrations are separate datasets and are not pooled into this report.

AgentDojo provides an extensible environment for studying prompt-injection attacks and defenses in agent tasks [1]. Northfield is much smaller: a single-step purchasing simulation focused on recorded actions and explicit authority. Its scope should be read as a complement for inspection and regression, not a substitute for broader adversarial evaluation.

CaMeL separates trusted control flow from untrusted data and applies capability-based policies to tool use [2]. Design Patterns for Securing LLM Agents against Prompt Injections describes broader structural defenses [3]. Northfield does not claim the guarantees of those systems. It illustrates a narrow execution boundary with public code and exposes an intent gap that the selected authority rules do not address.

Inspect offers composable tasks, agents, tools, scorers and evaluation logs [4]. Its emphasis on inspectable records is relevant to the next stage of this work. The present kit is a dependency-free runner rather than an Inspect integration. An integration should preserve the distinction between model failures, authority decisions and completion of valid tasks.

sections.heading: 8. Reproducing the work
paragraphs: The evidence bundle contains the fixed plan, three model reports, source hashes, the analysis script and kit 1.0.1. Each completed trial includes its input state, request, supporting text, proposal, both resulting ledgers, model identifier, latency and token usage. Failed slots remain listed in the report. File checksums detect changes; they are not independent signatures or attestations.

Replay recomputes outcomes from recorded proposals without calling a model. All three saved reports replayed with identical outcomes. The analysis script separately checks coverage of the 108 planned slots, source hashes, scenario inputs and recomputed results before generating the summary. A fresh model run is a new experiment and may produce different answers, even with the same model version.

Developers can replace the model adapter with their own agent. Expected answers and scripted fixtures are not sent to that adapter. The runner keeps credentials in the local environment and does not upload reports. The CI mode flags unauthorized execution, wrong recorded payments and valid tasks left uncompleted in the checked path. Passing it means passing this small suite, not being safe in general.

The next measurement improvement is to retain bounded, sanitized rejected outputs and their usage so formatting failures can be diagnosed. That change should be versioned and tested before a separately labeled replication. After that, independent contributed cases should guide expansion to shared-budget concurrency, changing authority and delegation. We have not yet measured external adoption or obtained an independent reproduction, so no product conclusion follows from this pilot.

sections.heading: 9. Disclosure and availability
paragraphs: This work was produced as a Delegus experiment. The author is affiliated with Delegus, whose interest in bounded-authority agent systems should be considered when interpreting the framing. This technical report has not been peer reviewed. No human-subject study, customer data or real financial transactions are included.

AI assistance was used for implementation, experiment orchestration, analysis code, visual design and drafting. The numerical results come from the released API-attempt records and deterministic analysis, not from generated example data. The checks described here are local verification, not independent review.

The report and study data are available under CC BY 4.0. Research kit code and scenarios retain their MIT license. Delegus branding and third-party assets are excluded from those grants. The companion lab is at lab.delegus.ai/research; the experiment repository is delegusai/northfield-challenge on GitHub. The Zenodo record identifies this version of the report and its evidence bundle.
